claims.text: Laser-assisted machining with controlled preheating and a TiAlN/SH-coated end mill will improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of high-entropy alloy components relative to conventional machining.
The intervention will produce a refined grain structure at the machined surface.
The intervention will reduce thermal stresses at the machined surface.
Laser preheating moderates thermal gradients during machining.
Moderating thermal gradients during machining minimizes thermal shock.
Moderating thermal gradients during machining minimizes residual-stress formation.
The controlled machining process will promote finer grains.
The controlled machining process may promote stable precipitate distributions.
The proposed microstructural modifications will enhance high-temperature mechanical strength.
The proposed microstructural modifications will enhance high-temperature creep resistance.
Elevated-temperature yield strength may increase by approximately 10–20% relative to conventionally machined specimens.
Creep resistance may improve by approximately 10–20% relative to conventionally machined specimens.
The predicted benefit should hold during sustained operation above approximately 600 °C.
The intervention is applicable to extreme-environment turbine and aerospace components.
The benefits may be limited or absent outside high, sustained-temperature service conditions.
Known effects of controlled thermal processing on microstructure qualitatively support the proposed mechanism.
